Text: To prevent {{c2::death or permanent disability::two outcomes}}, ensure your patient's airway remains {{c1::open (patent)::airway state}} and adequate.
Back Extra:
Cue: a patient of any age who is talking or crying has an open airway.

Pitfall: a conscious patient who cannot speak or cry most likely has a severe airway obstruction — stop the assessment process and work to clear the airway.

Text:
Opening an unresponsive patient's airway:

Any potential for trauma → the {{c1::jaw-thrust}} maneuver

If the {{c1::jaw-thrust}} fails to yield a patent airway, or trauma is ruled out → the {{c1::head tilt-chin lift}} maneuver
Back Extra:
Pitfall: in an unconscious patient the tongue often relaxes and falls to the back of the throat — address it first by positioning the airway, then with an oral or nasal airway.

Cue: dentures, blood clots, vomitus, mucus, and food can also obstruct, and are cleared manually or with suction.

Text: You find an unresponsive man crumpled at the base of a ladder. Which maneuver do you use first to open his airway? {{c1::The jaw-thrust maneuver}}
Back Extra:
Why: unresponsive patients may have experienced a traumatic event — any potential for trauma means jaw-thrust first.

Cue: switch to the head tilt-chin lift only if the jaw-thrust fails to give a patent airway, or trauma is confidently excluded.

Text:
In an unconscious patient, the signs of airway obstruction are:

{{c1::Obvious trauma, blood, or other obstruction}}

{{c1::Noisy breathing (snoring, bubbling, gurgling, crowing, stridor, or other abnormal sounds)}}

{{c1::Extremely shallow or absent breathing}}
Back Extra:
Cue: normal breathing is quiet — any added sound is obstruction until proven otherwise.

Why: with any of these present the airway is inadequate — open it (jaw-thrust if trauma is possible, otherwise head tilt-chin lift), suction, and place an airway adjunct as needed; an unmanaged airway starves the body of oxygen.

Text: A patient who is {{c2::breathing without assistance}} is said to have {{c1::spontaneous respirations::term}}.
Back Extra: Cue: three questions then judge those breaths — Is the patient breathing? Is the breathing adequate? Is the patient hypoxic?

Text:
In the primary assessment, the breathing findings decide the intervention:

Not breathing, or breathing too slow or too shallow → {{c1::provide positive-pressure ventilations::action}}

Breathing adequately but still hypoxic → {{c1::administer oxygen::action}}
Back Extra:
Cue: consider positive-pressure ventilations with an airway adjunct when respirations exceed 28 breaths/min with signs of distress, are fewer than 8 breaths/min, or are too shallow for adequate air exchange — air exchange, not the number of breaths, is the critical issue.

Pitfall: oxygen alone does nothing for a patient who is not moving air — inadequate breathing needs ventilation, not just supplemental O2.
verified_by: agent — 28 and 8 breaths/min verified verbatim on the p955 render (Back Extra cue); editor re-verified both digits on p955

Text: For most patients, the goal for oxygenation is an oxygen saturation of greater than {{c1::94}}%.
Back Extra:
Cue: breathing adequately but sitting below the goal = hypoxic — administer oxygen.

Pitfall: a good saturation number never overrides inadequate breathing — too-slow or too-shallow breathing still needs positive-pressure ventilations.
verified_by: agent — 94% verified verbatim on the p955 render; editor re-verified 'greater than 94%' on p955

Text: A calm woman is breathing at a normal rate with full, easy chest rise, but her oxygen saturation reads 90%. What do you do? {{c1::Administer oxygen::PPV or oxygen}}
Back Extra:
Why: her breathing is adequate, so she needs oxygenation, not ventilation — the goal is a saturation above 94%.

Distinguish: positive-pressure ventilations are reserved for absent, too-slow, or too-shallow breathing.
verified_by: agent — scenario built on the verified >94% goal from the p955 render; 90% is a below-goal exemplar value; editor re-verified the goal on p955

Text: {{c1::Shallow::depth descriptor}} respirations show {{c2::little movement of the chest wall}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: deep respirations cause a significant rise and fall of the chest — document either extreme.

Why: little chest movement = reduced tidal volume and poor chest excursion — each breath moves too little air, so even a normal rate can fail to provide adequate air exchange.

Text: {{c1::Retractions::sign}} are {{c2::indentations above the clavicles and between the ribs}} — like accessory-muscle use, a sign of inadequate breathing.
Back Extra:
Cue: watch how much effort breathing requires — retractions and accessory-muscle use mean the body is recruiting extra help to move air.

Distinguish: in pediatric patients the parallel signs are nasal flaring and seesaw breathing.

Text: A man's breathing is rapid but so shallow his chest barely moves; his neck muscles strain and the skin pulls in between his ribs with each breath. Beyond oxygen, what should you consider? {{c1::Positive-pressure ventilations (with an airway adjunct)::intervention}}
Back Extra:
Cue: retractions plus accessory-muscle use = inadequate breathing; too shallow to exchange air = ventilate.

Pitfall: a fast rate can look like the effort is working — air exchange, not the number of breaths, is the critical issue.

Text:
The accessory muscles of respiration are three groups:

{{c1::the neck muscles (sternocleidomastoid)}}

{{c1::the chest pectoralis major muscles}}

{{c1::the abdominal muscles}}
Back Extra: Cue: normal breathing is an effortless process — visible use of these groups is a sign of inadequate breathing, as are retractions.
verified_by: agent — closed 3-group list verified on the p955 render; editor re-verified: exactly neck (SCM), chest pectoralis major, abdominal

Text: In pediatric patients, {{c1::nasal flaring}} and {{c1::seesaw breathing}} indicate inadequate breathing.
Back Extra: Distinguish: retractions and accessory-muscle use flag inadequate breathing in general — flaring and seesaw breathing are the pediatric-specific tells.

Text: A patient sitting upright with the head and chin thrust slightly forward is in the {{c1::sniffing::posture}} position, seen most commonly in {{c2::children::age group}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the tripod position — sitting, leaning forward on outstretched arms — is the other airflow-maximizing posture, and demands significant conscious effort to breathe.

Why: patients in marked difficulty instinctively assume the posture that makes breathing easier.

Cue: the name is literal — the patient appears to be sniffing the air.

Cue: early tells are the patient's position, concentration on breathing, and increased effort and depth of each breath; as it worsens, chest and neck accessory muscles engage and the patient may grunt with each breath.

Ex: in infants and small children it commonly brings nasal flaring, supraclavicular and intercostal retractions, and sometimes gasping.

Text: Infants and small children may sustain labored breathing for a long period, but then often become {{c1::exhausted}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: a small child still working hard to breathe is on a clock — the crash comes when the effort runs out.

Why: once exhausted, they no longer have the strength to maintain the energy needed to breathe.

Cue: grunting, gasping, nasal flaring, and supraclavicular/intercostal retractions mark labored breathing in infants and small children.

Text: In infants and small children, cardiac arrest is generally caused by {{c1::respiratory arrest}}.
Back Extra:
Pathway: respiratory distress → respiratory failure → (uncorrected) respiratory arrest → cardiac arrest.

Why: breathing failure comes first in children — aggressive airway and ventilation care is what prevents the cardiac arrest.

Text:
As respiratory distress deteriorates into respiratory failure, the patient's whole drive winds down:

Agitation, anxiety, restlessness become {{c1::lethargy, difficult to rouse}}

Mild tachycardia becomes {{c1::bradycardia}}

Nasal flaring, seesaw breathing, head bobbing give way to {{c1::diminished muscle tone}}
Back Extra:
Why: distress means working harder to breathe (effort and rate up); failure means the work is no longer oxygenating the blood — the winding-down child is running out, not settling down.

Pitfall: an agitated child who seems to be "calming" may actually be slipping into failure — reassess, don't relax.

Roster: failure signs — lethargy/difficult to rouse · tachypnea with periods of bradypnea or agonal respirations · inadequate chest rise/poor excursion · inadequate respiratory rate or effort · bradycardia · diminished muscle tone

Text:
As respiratory distress deteriorates into respiratory failure, the breathing itself gives out:

Stridor and wheezing become {{c1::tachypnea with periods of bradypnea, or agonal respirations}}

Tachypnea becomes {{c1::an inadequate respiratory rate or effort}}

Accessory-muscle use with intercostal retractions and neck-muscle use becomes {{c1::inadequate chest rise / poor excursion}}
Back Extra:
Why: respiratory failure means the blood is inadequately oxygenated or ventilation cannot meet the body's oxygen demands — and uncorrected, its ultimate result is respiratory arrest.

Roster: failure signs — lethargy/difficult to rouse · tachypnea with periods of bradypnea or agonal respirations · inadequate chest rise/poor excursion · inadequate respiratory rate or effort · bradycardia · diminished muscle tone
